intuition: For each number, ask: what other number would make the target sum? Subtract the current number from the target to find that partner. Save earlier numbers and their positions in a dictionary. Then you can find the partner without trying every pair.

A dictionary converts that question into a fast lookup. Its keys are values and its entries remember indices, because the requested answer is positional. Before index i is processed, the dictionary contains only earlier elements. This small invariant makes the distinct-index rule automatic rather than something to repair afterward.

The order of operations is the important detail. Look for the complement first and insert the current value only after an unsuccessful lookup. With two equal values, the later copy can find the earlier copy; a lone value can never find itself. This works equally well for negatives and zero, since the reasoning uses addition rather than sorted order.

steps: The example has nums=[2,7,11,15] and target=9. Begin with an empty seen dictionary.
At i=0, value=2 requires complement=7. Seven has not appeared, so no pair can end at this index.
Record seen[2]=0. This stores an index, not a count or a boolean.
At i=1, value=7 requires complement=2. The dictionary now contains that value at index 0.
Return [0,1]: the indices are distinct and their values 2+7 equal 9. The remaining numbers need no examination.

codeNotes.note: The dictionary represents the processed prefix. Keeping only earlier indices gives every successful lookup a valid distinct partner.
Subtraction identifies one exact lookup target, replacing the entire inner loop over possible partners.
Insertion follows the lookup. Reversing those operations could incorrectly reuse the current element when target is twice its value.

keyDecision: Look for the partner before saving the current number. This prevents using the same position twice.

figures.title: Find the missing partner
figures.caption: Use the example target 9. Small labels show array indices, not the values to return.

panels.title: Before: save the first number
panels.note: For value 2, the needed 7 is not saved yet. Save 2 at index 0.

panels.title: Check: read the next number
panels.note: For value 7, calculate 9 - 7 = 2. The saved map contains 2.

panels.title: After: return two positions
panels.note: Positions 0 and 1 are different, and their values add to 9.

concept.question: What if each number could ask for its missing partner?
intuition: Imagine four number tiles and a target total of nine. We need two different tiles that fill that total exactly. Trying every pair works, but each new tile makes us revisit the earlier tiles one by one. The question becomes much simpler when we turn it around: if this tile is seven, which single value would complete nine?

The missing partner is two. Keep a small address book of numbers already encountered and their positions. Looking up two now answers the whole pairing question in one operation. This is the useful observation: a search through many possible partners can become a question about one exact value.
concept.observation: Ask for the missing partner before remembering the current tile. The address book then contains only different, earlier positions.
approach: Read a number and subtract it from the target to find the missing partner.
Look for that partner among earlier numbers. If it is there, the two remembered positions are the answer.
If it is absent, remember this number and its position, then continue.
concept.correctness: Every valid pair has an earlier tile and a later tile. When the later one arrives, the earlier one is already remembered. Their values make the target by construction. Since the current tile has not yet entered the address book, it cannot accidentally pair with itself. This explains both why every valid pair can be found and why a reported pair uses two different positions.

complexity.explanation: Read each tile at most once. Looking up and remembering a value take constant time on average, so doubling the number of tiles roughly doubles the work. The address book may need to remember almost all the tiles. Hashing gives an expected, rather than worst-case, linear time bound.

pitfalls: Two equal values can form a pair only when they occupy two separate positions.
The answer is a pair of positions, not the two number values.
Negative numbers and zero follow exactly the same missing-partner reasoning.

illustrations.alt: Two glowing puzzle pieces join into one outline, suggesting a number and its missing partner.
illustrations.caption: Think of each number as one piece of a target total. Its missing piece must come from another position; the exact example beside this lesson pairs 2 with 7.

scenes.title: Two tiles, one total
scenes.narration: The numbers are 2, 7, 11, and 15. Find two different positions whose values make 9.
scenes.decision: A tile can contribute once. We are finding positions, not creating new numbers.

scenes.title: Why checking every pair repeats work
scenes.narration: We could compare 2 with 7, then 11, then 15, and repeat such comparisons for every next number.
scenes.decision: Those repeated comparisons are the bottleneck. We want to ask a more focused question.

scenes.title: Turn the question around
scenes.narration: For each number, ask what is missing from 9. For 2, the missing partner is 7.
scenes.decision: Only one value can complete a particular number to the target.

scenes.title: Remember the first tile
scenes.narration: No earlier number is available yet. Remember the value 2 and its position, 0.
scenes.decision: Remembering its position lets us later return the location of the pair.

scenes.title: The next tile finds its partner
scenes.narration: The next value is 7. Its missing partner is 2, already remembered at position 0.
scenes.decision: The stored tile is earlier, so these are two different positions.

scenes.title: The answer emerges
scenes.narration: Positions 0 and 1 hold 2 and 7. Their total is 9, so these positions are the answer.
scenes.decision: The required pair is found. The remaining numbers cannot improve an exact answer.

scenes.title: Why no pair is missed
scenes.narration: In any valid pair, the later tile asks for the earlier tile. The earlier tile is waiting in the address book.
scenes.decision: One forward scan eventually examines the later member of the guaranteed pair.

scenes.title: A useful boundary case
scenes.narration: Separate example: a target of 6 with two tiles both valued 3 is valid. A single tile valued 3 cannot be used twice.
scenes.decision: Check before remembering the current tile to preserve the distinct-position rule.
